text:
# Build a brand

Run the steps in order; each step's output is the next step's input. Pull the step's shelf before you start it.

1. **brd-004 Creative brief** from a discovery questionnaire (no public gold: required shape + judge)
2. **brd-003 Competitive landscape** (search Brand New, Logobook)
3. **brd-001 Brand platform** (low gold: the Collins strategy sentence is the move)
4. **brd-006 Logo and wordmark** — or **brd-010** if refreshing an existing mark
5. **brd-011 Type** and **brd-012 Color**
6. **brd-014 Guidelines**
7. **brd-017 Voice and tone**
8. **brd-050 Rationale** to launch it

**Keep one system.** If you pick an exemplar for step 4, follow its `same_system` links for later steps
before mixing sources: Mailchimp's identity, brand page and content style guide are one coherent system.
title: Build a brand

# Dropbox Brand Guidelines

**Why it's gold**
- A digital-first guidelines *site*: eight sections from Framework and Voice & Tone through Motion, which the
  print-era NASA manual can't cover.
- Puts partner and legal resources at the top, so external users find what they need first.

**Weakness**
- Only the index was read for this entry; logo construction detail lives on sub-pages not yet reviewed.

**Use when** writing guidelines for a software brand that lives mostly on screens.

text:
# IBM 8-bar logo — Paul Rand, 1972

**Why it's gold**
- One device carries the whole identity: the letters set in eight (sometimes 13) horizontal bars.
- Works in a single color; IBM's own history page shows it in black, gray, white or IBM Blue.
- Part of a lineage Rand managed: he drew the 1956 version, the 1972 bars and the 1981 rebus poster, so the
  mark evolved instead of being replaced.
- Fifty-plus years in use with only color and context adjusted.

**Weakness**
- Fine bars thin out at small sizes; check a 16px favicon version separately.
- The page is a history, not a construction spec: no grid, clear space or minimum size.

**Use when** an established company wants a typographic mark that must survive one-color reproduction.
title: IBM 8-bar logo
verified: 2026-11-05 page fetched, title "The IBM logo | IBM"

text:
# "Write issues not user stories" — Linear

**Why it's gold** (for a small change)
- "Write only as much as you need to share to perform the task and communicate relevant information."
- Short, direct titles that state the task.
- Argues user stories "obscure the work to be done" by pulling product-level detail into the task level, which
  is exactly the over-writing a full PRD template pushes onto a tweak.

**Weakness**
- Guidance, not a worked example spec.

**Use when** the change is a tweak; step up to pm-007 only if it needs goals, non-goals and metrics.
title: "Write issues not user stories" (Linear Method)

text:
# Mailchimp brand assets — the minimal public page

**Why it's gold** (for the small job)
- Everything a partner or journalist needs on one page: the name ("one word, spelled with a big M and a little
  c"), always pair the name with Freddie, use the reverse version on dark, two named colors (Cavendish Yellow,
  Peppercorn), and four plain don'ts.

**Weakness**
- Not a guidelines system: no hex values, no construction, no type. Using it as the model for a full
  guidelines document would under-deliver; see the contrast with the NASA manual.

**Use when** you need a press kit or public brand page (brd-015), not internal guidelines.
title: Mailchimp brand assets page

text:
# Mailchimp brand system — COLLINS

**Why it's gold**
- Starts from a business problem, not taste: email credibility "wasn't translating elsewhere", which blocked
  cross-selling 35 added products.
- The brand idea is a strategy sentence: "Fuel small and midsize businesses growth by democratizing
  cutting-edge marketing technology."
- Fixes the architecture (35 solutions into five categories) *before* the visual system.
- One ownable visual move: a hallmark illustration style inspired by outsider art, embracing "imperfection and
  a hand-drawn aesthetic", on a yellow-heavy palette.

**Weakness**
- Case-study page, not the full system; no rejected directions. Year not stated on the page.

**Use when** a rebrand is really a portfolio or positioning problem (brd-001), not just a logo refresh.
title: Mailchimp brand system case study

facets: pages=60; sections=logotype, color, incorrect uses, grid drawing, reproduction art per center, ...
text:
# NASA Graphics Standards Manual — Danne & Blackburn, 1976

**Why it's gold**
- Opens on the logotype (the "worm") and then defines everything that depends on it, in order: agency and
  center identification, the NASA color, use of color, color standards.
- Has an explicit **"The Logotype: Incorrect Uses"** page (1.6) and a **grid drawing for large applications**
  (1.7). Rules come with the drawings needed to follow them.
- Ships **reproduction art for every center** (Ames, Goddard, JPL, Johnson, Kennedy, Langley, ...): the
  manual solves the multi-unit problem, not just the logo.

**Weakness**
- Print-era: no screen, motion, accessibility or digital-product guidance.

**Use when** writing guidelines for an organisation with many teams or sub-brands that must stay consistent.
Also the best public example of a logo shipped *with* its construction grid and misuse page (brd-006).
title: NASA Graphics Standards Manual (NHB 1430.2)
verified: 2026-11-05 PDF fetched, 60 pages, title "NASA Graphics Standards Manual (NHB 1430.2) (January 1976)"

text:
# "Write the Pitch" — Shape Up

**Why it's gold**
- Five ingredients with definitions: problem, **appetite** ("how much time we want to spend and how that
  constrains the solution"), solution, **rabbit holes**, **no-gos**.
- Includes two real pitches from Basecamp, so the agent sees finished work, not a template.

**Weakness**
- Assumes a six-week cycle culture; teams without fixed appetites may skip the hard part.

**Use when** the team works in fixed time budgets and the question is "what fits in the time we'll spend".

text:
# Slack logo refresh — Pentagram, 2019

**Why it's gold**
- Names the old mark's failure concretely: eleven colors that "suffered against any background color other
  than white", reproduction problems, inconsistency.
- **Keeps the equity** (the octothorpe) and rebuilds it on a grid from two shapes, a speech bubble and a
  lozenge, which then become the system's graphic elements.
- Cuts the palette to four screen-optimized primaries and keeps aubergine as the accent.
- Built to "scale up or down to optimize legibility at various sizes."
- The logo is the first piece of a system: icons, illustrations and rounded-corner motifs from the same shapes.

**Weakness**
- The case study shows outcomes, not rejected directions; you can't see the search.

**Use when** refreshing a mark people already recognise, especially one that breaks on non-white backgrounds.
title: Slack logo and identity refresh

facets: length=short blog post; states=old problems, what was kept, what changed
text:
# "Say hello, new logo" — Slack, 2019

**Why it's gold**
- The rationale customers read: old logo "hard to get right" (11 colors, a prescribed 18º rotation), variant
  versions that didn't match, recognition suffering.
- Says what was kept ("the spirit of the original", the hash that matches the channel marker) before what
  changed, which is how you announce a refresh without alarming existing users.

**Weakness**
- Marketing voice; no construction detail. Pair it with the Pentagram case study.

**Use when** writing the public rationale for a logo change (brd-050).
title: "Say hello, new logo" (Slack's rationale post)

text:
# Homebrew Security Assessment — Trail of Bits

**Why it's gold**
- States scope and effort up front (six engineer-weeks; core package manager, CI/CD, the JSON API) and has
  explicit **Project Coverage** and **Automated Testing** sections, so the reader knows what was *not* looked at.
- A **Codebase Maturity Evaluation** separate from the findings: the system's habits, not just its bugs.
- Findings grouped by impact in the summary ("escape the build sandbox", "compromise the CI/CD workflow"),
  each with a stable ID (TOB-BREW-2, ...).
- Recommends the class fix as well as the instances: **"Document Homebrew's security model"** — what is trusted
  (core formulae) and what isn't (third-party formulae, casks).

**Weakness**
- Time-boxed; the report itself says it is not a comprehensive list.

**Use when** auditing an installer, package manager or any tool that runs or writes third-party content.
title: Homebrew Security Assessment
verified: 2026-11-05 PDF fetched and read (contents, executive summary)

by: Colin Bryar and Bill Carr (Working Backwards)
facets: sections=heading, subheading, summary, problem, solution, quotes and getting started, external FAQ, internal FAQ
text:
# Working Backwards PR/FAQ

**Why it's gold**
- Forces the customer's view first: a one-sentence heading and subheading, then the problem "from the
  customer's point of view", then how this differs from current alternatives.
- Splits FAQs into **external** (customers, press) and **internal** (leaders and every department: technical,
  financial, legal, operational problems to solve).
- "Designed to be lightweight": a first draft should take a few hours.

**Weakness**
- Built for new products; overkill for a feature on an existing surface (use pm-007 or pm-051).

**Use when** the idea is a new product or a bet that needs a yes from leadership.
title: Working Backwards PR/FAQ instructions and template
